- operations:capacity-plan: Plan resource capacity — workload analysis and utilization forecasting. Use when heading into quarterly planning, the team feels overallocated and you need the numbers, deciding whether to hire or deprioritize, or stress-testing whether upcoming projects fit the people you have.
- operations:change-request: Create a change management request with impact analysis and rollback plan. Use when proposing a system or process change that needs approval, preparing a change record for CAB review, documenting risk and rollback steps before a deployment, or planning stakeholder communications for a rollout.
- operations:compliance-tracking: Track compliance requirements and audit readiness. Trigger with "compliance", "audit prep", "SOC 2", "ISO 27001", "GDPR", "regulatory requirement", or when the user needs help tracking, preparing for, or documenting compliance activities.
- operations:process-doc: Document a business process — flowcharts, RACI, and SOPs. Use when formalizing a process that lives in someone's head, building a RACI to clarify who owns what, writing an SOP for a handoff or audit, or capturing the exceptions and edge cases of how work actually gets done.
- operations:process-optimization: Analyze and improve business processes. Trigger with "this process is slow", "how can we improve", "streamline this workflow", "too many steps", "bottleneck", or when the user describes an inefficient process they want to fix.
- operations:risk-assessment: Identify, assess, and mitigate operational risks. Trigger with "what are the risks", "risk assessment", "risk register", "what could go wrong", or when the user is evaluating risks associated with a project, vendor, process, or decision.
- operations:runbook: Create or update an operational runbook for a recurring task or procedure. Use when documenting a task that on-call or ops needs to run repeatably, turning tribal knowledge into exact step-by-step commands, adding troubleshooting and rollback steps to an existing procedure, or writing escalation paths for when things go wrong.
- operations:status-report: Generate a status report with KPIs, risks, and action items. Use when writing a weekly or monthly update for leadership, summarizing project health with green/yellow/red status, surfacing risks and decisions that need stakeholder attention, or turning a pile of project tracker activity into a readable narrative.
- operations:vendor-review: Evaluate a vendor — cost analysis, risk assessment, and recommendation. Use when reviewing a new vendor proposal, deciding whether to renew or replace a contract, comparing two vendors side-by-side, or building a TCO breakdown and negotiation points before procurement sign-off.
- design:accessibility-review: Run a WCAG 2.1 AA accessibility audit on a design or page. Trigger with "audit accessibility", "check a11y", "is this accessible?", or when reviewing a design for color contrast, keyboard navigation, touch target size, or screen reader behavior before handoff.
- design:design-critique: Get structured design feedback on usability, hierarchy, and consistency. Trigger with "review this design", "critique this mockup", "what do you think of this screen?", or when sharing a Figma link or screenshot for feedback at any stage from exploration to final polish.
- design:design-handoff: Generate developer handoff specs from a design. Use when a design is ready for engineering and needs a spec sheet covering layout, design tokens, component props, interaction states, responsive breakpoints, edge cases, and animation details.
- design:design-system: Audit, document, or extend your design system. Use when checking for naming inconsistencies or hardcoded values across components, writing documentation for a component's variants, states, and accessibility notes, or designing a new pattern that fits the existing system.
- design:research-synthesis: Synthesize user research into themes, insights, and recommendations. Use when you have interview transcripts, survey results, usability test notes, support tickets, or NPS responses that need to be distilled into patterns, user segments, and prioritized next steps.
- design:user-research: Plan, conduct, and synthesize user research. Trigger with "user research plan", "interview guide", "usability test", "survey design", "research questions", or when the user needs help with any aspect of understanding their users through research.
- design:ux-copy: Write or review UX copy — microcopy, error messages, empty states, CTAs. Trigger with "write copy for", "what should this button say?", "review this error message", or when naming a CTA, wording a confirmation dialog, filling an empty state, or writing onboarding text.
- engineering:architecture: Create or evaluate an architecture decision record (ADR). Use when choosing between technologies (e.g., Kafka vs SQS), documenting a design decision with trade-offs and consequences, reviewing a system design proposal, or designing a new component from requirements and constraints.
- engineering:code-review: Review code changes for security, performance, and correctness. Trigger with a PR URL or diff, "review this before I merge", "is this code safe?", or when checking a change for N+1 queries, injection risks, missing edge cases, or error handling gaps.
- engineering:debug: Structured debugging session — reproduce, isolate, diagnose, and fix. Trigger with an error message or stack trace, "this works in staging but not prod", "something broke after the deploy", or when behavior diverges from expected and the cause isn't obvious.
- engineering:deploy-checklist: Pre-deployment verification checklist. Use when about to ship a release, deploying a change with database migrations or feature flags, verifying CI status and approvals before going to production, or documenting rollback triggers ahead of time.

- engineering:incident-response: Run an incident response workflow — triage, communicate, and write postmortem. Trigger with "we have an incident", "production is down", an alert that needs severity assessment, a status update mid-incident, or when writing a blameless postmortem after resolution.

# CLAUDE.md – ÖKOVOLT NetOps

Projektanweisung für Claude Code. Vor jeder Arbeit vollständig lesen.
Fachkonzept: https://claude.ai/artifact/PaFDHFySgCJKyP4yut5NGP

## 1. Projekt

Zentrale Plattform für Netzwerkdokumentation, Betrieb und Cybersicherheit der ÖKOVOLT-Gruppe.
Führendes System (Single Source of Truth für das Soll). Angebundene Systeme liefern das Ist.

**Architekturentscheidung (verbindlich):** Kein NetBox, kein IT Glue, kein Hudu.
Die App bildet DCIM, IPAM und strukturierte Dokumentation vollständig selbst ab.
Das Datenmodell orientiert sich an NetBox, damit Import/Export (NetBox-kompatibles JSON/CSV) möglich bleibt.

## 2. Stack

- Frappe Framework v15, MariaDB, Redis, Frappe Realtime (Socket.IO)
- Frontend: Vue 3 + Vite + frappe-ui, eigene SPA unter `/netops`, Leitstand unter `/screen1`–`/screen10`
- Topologie: Cytoscape.js oder Vue Flow
- Zeitreihen/Logs später: ClickHouse (nicht in MariaDB)
- Python ≥ 3.11, Node ≥ 20
- App-Name: `netops`

## 3. Konventionen

- DocType- und Feldnamen intern **englisch** (`network_device`, `ip_address`), Labels und UI **deutsch** über Übersetzungen.
- Jeder DocType: `tenant` (Link Mandant), `status`, `description`, Änderungsverfolgung an (`track_changes`).
- Beziehungen über Link/Dynamic Link, nie über Freitext.
- Keine Geschäftslogik im Frontend; Prüfungen serverseitig (Controller, Validierungen).
- Whitelisted API-Methoden nur mit expliziter Rechteprüfung (`frappe.has_permission`), nie `allow_guest`, außer der Screen-Warteseite (siehe 7).
- Tests: `bench run-tests --app netops` muss grün sein, bevor eine Aufgabe als erledigt gilt.
- Commits klein, deutschsprachige Commit-Messages, ein Thema pro Commit.

## 4. Datenmodell Phase 1 (DocTypes)

**Organisation**
- `Tenant` (Mandant): Gesellschaft, Land, Domain(s)
- `Site` (Baum): Standort → Gebäude → Raum; Adresse, Grundriss (Attach)
- `Contact`-Nutzung von Frappe; `Provider`, `Supplier`-Verweis

**DCIM**
- `Manufacturer`, `Device Type` (Hersteller, Modell, HE, Kind-Tabellen: Interface-/Power-/Front-/Rear-Port-Vorlagen)
- `Device Role`
- `Rack`: Site, Höhe in HE, Nummerierung, max. Gewicht/Last
- `Network Device`: Typ, Rolle, Site, Rack, Position/Seite, Seriennummer, Asset-Nr., Firmware, Garantie-/Support-Ende, Management-IP, Verantwortlicher (User), Lebenszyklus-Status, Passbolt-Referenz (nur ID/URL)
- `Device Interface`: Gerät, Name, Typ, MAC, Speed, Modus (access/tagged/tagged-all), Untagged-VLAN, Tagged-VLANs (Kind-Tabelle), LAG-Parent, PoE, aktiv
- `Front Port`, `Rear Port` (Patchfelder), `Power Port`, `Power Outlet`, `Power Feed`
- `Cable`: A-Ende und B-Ende (Dynamic Link auf Interface/Front Port/Rear Port/Power Port/Outlet/Wall Outlet), Typ, Farbe, Länge, Label, Status
- `Wall Outlet` (Dose): Raum, Bezeichnung
- Kabel-Trace als serverseitige Methode (`trace_path(endpoint)`)

**IPAM**
- `VRF`, `Security Zone`, `VLAN Group`, `VLAN` (VID, Name, Zone, Zweck)
- `IP Prefix` (Baum über Parent-Berechnung): Präfix, VRF, VLAN, Rolle, Site, Auslastung (berechnet)
- `IP Range` (DHCP/Pools), `IP Address`: Adresse/Maske, VRF, zugewiesenes Interface (Dynamic Link), DNS-Name, Rolle, Status
- Validierung: keine Dubletten je VRF, IP muss in einem Präfix liegen (Warnung, nicht Fehler)

**Dokumentation (IT-Glue/Hudu-Umfang)**
- `NetOps Document`: Typ (Netzplan, SOP, Runbook, Notfallplan, Wartungsprotokoll, Konfigurationsstand), Inhalt (Text Editor), Anhänge, Version, Freigabestatus
- `Object Relation`: Von (Dynamic Link) → Nach (Dynamic Link), Beziehungstyp (hängt ab von, läuft auf, dokumentiert, ersetzt …)
- `Checklist Template` + `Checklist Run` (Punkte abhaken, Pflichtpunkte, Nachweis)
- `Contract` (Laufzeit, Kündigungsfrist, Kosten, verknüpfte Objekte), `License`
- `Access Reference`: nur Verweis auf Passbolt-Eintrag (ID, URL, Bezeichnung) – **niemals Geheimnisse**

**Betrieb/Audit**
- `Audit Entry` (append-only): Zeit, Benutzer, Aktion, Objekt, Payload-Hash, `prev_hash`, `entry_hash` (SHA-256 über prev_hash + Inhalt). Kein Update/Delete (Controller verbietet es).
- `Connector`, `Connector Run`, `Raw Snapshot` (Rohdaten + Hash), `Drift Finding` (Soll/Ist-Abweichung, Status: offen/übernommen/verworfen)

## 5. Konnektor-Vertrag

Jeder Konnektor ist eine Klasse unter `netops/connectors/<name>.py`:

```python
class Connector:
    def health(self) -> dict: ...
    def pull(self) -> dict: ...                # Rohdaten, unverändert
    def normalize(self, raw: dict) -> list: ...# normierte Objekte
    # apply(change) existiert in Phase 1 NICHT
```

- Rohdaten immer als `Raw Snapshot` speichern (mit SHA-256), dann normalisieren.
- Normalisierte Objekte **nie direkt** ins Soll schreiben: Unterschiede erzeugen `Drift Finding`.
- Zugangsdaten nur über `netops.secrets.get(name)` – Phase 1 liest aus Umgebungsvariablen/`site_config` (Platzhalter), später OpenBao. Keine Tokens im Code, in DocTypes oder Logs.
- Timeouts, Retry mit Backoff, TLS-Prüfung an (eigene CA konfigurierbar, `verify=False` verboten).

**MVP-Konnektoren (nur lesen):** OPNsense, Proxmox VE, Proxmox Backup Server.

## 6. Sicherheitsregeln (nicht verhandelbar)

1. Entwicklung nur auf Test-Bench, keine Produktivdaten.
2. Nur Lese-Tokens. **Nie** Schreibzugriff auf die Perimeter-Firewall FW-OS-01 – weder im Code noch in Tests.
3. PBS-Token ohne Lösch-/Prune-Rechte.
4. Keine Geheimnisse in Repo, DocTypes, Logs, Fehlermeldungen oder Tests. `.env` in `.gitignore`.
5. Keine Befehle ausführen, die Konfigurationen an Firewalls, Switches, Hypervisor oder Backup ändern.
6. Keine Scans (nmap o. Ä.) im Netz ohne ausdrückliche Anweisung von Benny – eigene Scans müssen beim Wachhund angemeldet werden.
7. Abhängigkeiten nur aus offiziellen Quellen, `pip-audit`/`npm audit` vor jedem Merge.
8. Bei Unklarheit zu Rechten oder Zugriffen: anhalten und fragen.

## 7. MVP-Umfang (erste Sessions)

1. App `netops` anlegen, DocTypes Phase 1, Rollen: `NetOps Leser`, `NetOps Techniker`, `NetOps Security`, `NetOps Freigeber`, `NetOps Admin`, `Leitstand Anzeige`.
2. Audit-Hash-Kette inkl. Prüfmethode `verify_chain()` und Test.
3. Vue-SPA: Layout (Seitenleiste wie Mockup), globale Suche Strg+K (IP, MAC, Hostname, Seriennummer, Label, VLAN, Dose), Geräteliste, Gerätedetail mit Tabs, IPAM-Baum mit Auslastung.
4. Konnektoren OPNsense, Proxmox VE, PBS + Scheduler + Drift-Ansicht.
5. Backup-Ampel je VM/Dienst aus PBS (letztes Backup, Verify-Status, Alter).
6. **Leitstand `/screen1`** mit Freigabe-Ablauf:
   - Aufruf ohne Freigabe → Warteseite mit Bestätigungscode (6–8 Zeichen, 5 Min gültig), keine Daten.
   - Anfrage nur aus konfigurierten Leitstand-Subnetzen, sonst 403 + Audit-Eintrag.
   - `Screen Pairing Request` in der App, Freigabe durch Rolle `NetOps Admin` (Step-up-Hook vorsehen, FIDO2 folgt mit privacyIDEA).
   - Nach Freigabe: gerätegebundenes Token als HttpOnly/Secure/SameSite=Strict-Cookie, **nie** in der URL; nur Lesen, nur zugewiesener Screen.
   - Widerruf wirkt sofort (Realtime-Event), Herzschlag je Screen, veraltete Daten sichtbar markieren.
7. Offline-Export (JSON + CSV aller Kern-DocTypes) als Befehl `bench --site <site> netops-export`.

## 8. Fertig heißt

- Tests grün, keine offenen `pip-audit`/`npm audit`-Funde mit hoher Kritikalität.
- Jeder Konnektor läuft gegen die echte Testumgebung durch, `health()` grün.
- Audit-Kette verifiziert.
- Kurze Änderungsnotiz in `CHANGELOG.md`.

Claude publishes it, as an Artifact or through a first-party document connector when one is attached, and gives the person the link, so they have a private page ready to share when they choose. **To update an artifact from an earlier conversation**, Claude passes that artifact's URL as `url`. asset_ids.description: publish with `asset: true` and `from_url` only: 1–10 distinct asset ids from the source artifact (from a `scope: "assets"` listing of it, or an upload result).

favicon.description: Deprecated; Claude omits it and uses `icon`.

icon.description: One short generic word for the artifact's browser-tab icon, such as chart, calendar, recipe, code or map: a plain signifier, never a product or brand name. Claude includes it on every page's first publish and omits it on a redeploy so the artifact keeps its icon, passing a new one only when the person asks.

files.description: Supporting files to publish alongside the page, as a map {"published/path": "source/path" | {from, contentType} | {artifact, path, ver?} | null}. The key is what the HTML references. The source is a path on disk, or {from, contentType} when the type cannot be inferred from the published extension. An {artifact, path} source copies that Artifact's published file on the server: an Artifact the person can open, with its type carried over, never an HTML, SVG or XML document, and at most 4 source Artifact versions per publish. null removes that path on an update, and files left out are kept. A plain list publishes each file at its own spelling. Sources must be under the working directory or Claude's scratchpad directory. `preflight.js` at the artifact root is reserved: it runs against open pages when Claude publishes updates, and it must be a JavaScript module of at most 8 KiB whose default export is a function, or the publish is refused.

path.description: Path relative to the working directory (or to `root`, which may be a folder in your scratchpad directory); the file is served at this same path next to the page.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the extension for common types (css/js/json/png/…) — pass explicitly otherwise.

from.description: Source file path — relative to `root` (default: the working directory), or absolute under the working directory or your scratchpad directory.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the PUBLISHED extension for common types — pass explicitly otherwise.

artifact.description: Another artifact's claude.ai URL: the file is copied from ITS published files, server side — nothing is downloaded. You must be able to open that artifact.

path.description: The file's published path inside that Artifact, as a listing of its files prints it (not "index.html").

ver.description: A version of that Artifact to copy from instead of its current one — only versions you are served (its history, if you can edit it); omit for the current version.

root.description: The base directory that relative `files` sources resolve against, like a bundler root. It never changes published paths. It is relative to the working directory, or absolute within it or within Claude's scratchpad directory. It requires `files`.

pin.description: publish only: true also pins the published artifact to the person's claude.ai sidebar once it is published. Claude passes it only when the person asked for that. A failed pin never fails the publish, and the result says so.

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

scope.description: list: which listing to return. 'mine' is the default. The others are 'shared', 'all', 'files' (with `url`) and 'assets' (with `url`, continued with `after`). See **Calls**.

title.description: publish: the fallback title for an HTML page whose file has no <title>. It is a name, not a summary, and Claude keeps it the same across redeploys.

description.description: publish: one sentence for the subtitle on the gallery card.

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

overwrite_unread.description: publish with `files` or `root` to an existing artifact: published paths this call may replace or remove although you have not read or listed them in this session. Every other path the call touches must be one you read by its `path`, saw in a file listing, or published yourself, and must not have changed since — otherwise nothing is sent and the refusal names each path. Name a path here only when the user asked for it to be replaced without looking at what is there; it never excuses a path that changed after you read it.

url.description: An existing artifact's claude.ai link (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}); a chat, project or session link is not one, and `action: "list"` lists the person's artifacts. On a publish, it is the artifact to update in place, one the person owns or was given edit access to (a read of it says "writer"). Before publishing to an artifact this conversation has neither read nor published, Claude reads it (`action: "read"`) and builds on what comes back; a publish sent without that read is refused. A refusal that hands Claude the live version counts as that read: Claude merges its changes into that version and publishes the result, and never resends the refused content unchanged. Claude omits `url` for a new artifact or to redeploy a file this conversation already published. For read, delete and the other calls that take a URL, it is the artifact to act on.

prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the person: what Claude needs from it, which steers the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. On a conflict, Claude merges its changes onto the newer content that the rejection hands it and publishes again. Claude passes true only when the person explicitly said to discard that specific version, and the server may still refuse it over a version saved from inside the page.

out_dir.description: read with `path`: the directory to save into. The default is this artifact's folder in Claude's scratchpad directory, where saving needs no approval. A published file lands at <out_dir>/<published path>, and saving it outside that default folder asks the person first. An asset's file is named by its id plus its type's extension; saving it outside the default folder is an ordinary file save the person may be asked to approve.

path.description: read: the file's published path inside the artifact, exactly as a 'files' listing printed it ("index.html" is the page itself). The file is saved locally, the result says where, and a small text file's contents are included. It can instead be an uploaded asset's id (32 hex characters, from an 'assets' listing or an upload result), and that asset is saved to a local file. delete: the id of the one asset to remove.

paths.description: read: several published paths in place of `path`, up to 256 in one call. Each file is saved as a single `path` would be, and the result lists where each one landed, or why it could not be read, with small text files' contents included while they fit.

after.description: list with scope 'assets' only: the `next` value from a previous listing, passed to continue it.

capabilities.description: publish: the runtime capabilities this page declares, as {name: config}. Claude loads the `artifact-capabilities` skill before passing it. On a redeploy Claude omits the field to keep what the page has, and {} clears it.

contract.description: publish: the artifact's runtime version. Leaving it out keeps the current version (the default), 'latest' upgrades, and an exact version pins or rolls back. It changes how the published page behaves, so Claude passes it only when the author explicitly intends that change.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

This tool runs Git Bash (POSIX sh), not cmd.exe or PowerShell. Use Unix shell syntax: `/dev/null` not `NUL`, forward slashes, `$VAR` not `%VAR%` or `$env:VAR`. Do not use PowerShell here-strings (`@'…'@`) or backtick continuation here — for multi-line strings use a heredoc.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

schema.name: Edit
schema.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to modify

new_string.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from old_string)

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences of old_string (default false)

tools.name: Glob
tools.description: Fast file pattern matching. Supports glob patterns like "**/*.js" or "src/**/*.ts". Returns matching file paths sorted by modification time.

schema.name: Glob
schema.description: Fast file pattern matching. Supports glob patterns like "**/*.js" or "src/**/*.ts". Returns matching file paths sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: The glob pattern to match files against

path.description: The directory to search in. If not specified, the current working directory will be used. IMPORTANT: Omit this field to use the default directory. DO NOT enter "undefined" or "null" - simply omit it for the default behavior. Must be a valid directory path if provided.

tools.name: Grep
tools.description:
Content search built on ripgrep. Prefer this over `grep`/`rg` via Bash — results integrate with the permission UI and file links.

- Full regex syntax (e.g. "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+"). Ripgrep, not grep — escape literal braces (`interface\{\}`).
- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").
- `output_mode`: "content" (matching lines), "files_with_matches" (paths only, default), or "count".
- `multiline: true` for patterns that span lines.

schema.name: Grep
schema.description:
Content search built on ripgrep. Prefer this over `grep`/`rg` via Bash — results integrate with the permission UI and file links.

- Full regex syntax (e.g. "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+"). Ripgrep, not grep — escape literal braces (`interface\{\}`).
- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").
- `output_mode`: "content" (matching lines), "files_with_matches" (paths only, default), or "count".
- `multiline: true` for patterns that span lines.

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: Windows PowerShell 5.1 (powershell.exe)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` are NOT available — they cause a parser error. To run B only if A succeeds: `A; if ($?) { B }`. To chain unconditionally: `A; B`.
   - Ternary (`?:`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are NOT available. Use `if/else` and explicit `$null -eq` checks instead.
   - Avoid `2>&1` on native executables. In 5.1, redirecting a native command's stderr inside PowerShell wraps each line in an ErrorRecord (NativeCommandError) and sets `$?` to `$false` even when the exe returned exit code 0. stderr is already captured for you — don't redirect it.
   - `>`, `>>`, and `Out-File` usually default to UTF-8 (with BOM) in this environment, but `Set-Content`/`Add-Content` still default to the system ANSI codepage — when writing a file other tools will read, pass `-Encoding utf8` explicitly to `Out-File`/`Set-Content`.
   - `ConvertFrom-Json` returns a PSCustomObject, not a hashtable. `-AsHashtable` is not available.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

description.description: Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice.

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

Deliver your final report to the agent that spawned you (your caller). Use it once, for that hand-off only: when your work is complete, call SubagentHandback({message: <your full report>}) as your last tool call and then stop. ## claude.ai Figma
The official Figma MCP server. Use this server whenever the user wants to create, generate, edit, implement, or sync any design, UI, screen, component, mockup, or visual — in Figma, FigJam, Figma Make, or Figma Slides — and whenever the user mentions Figma or provides a figma.com URL.

This server bridges code and design in both directions, and supports designing from scratch using existing design systems and codebases.

CAPABILITIES:
- Read designs FROM Figma into code (get_design_context, get_screenshot, get_metadata, get_figjam)
- Write designs INTO Figma from code, intent, or existing components (use_figma, generate_figma_design, create_new_file, upload_assets)
- Bridge code and design via Code Connect (get_code_connect_map, add_code_connect_map)
- Create diagrams and FigJam content (generate_diagram, get_figjam)

WHEN TO USE THESE TOOLS:
- The user wants to create, mock up, or generate any UI, screen, component, or design — even if Figma isn't named
- The user wants to implement a design as code (design-to-code)
- The user wants to push a page, view, or component into Figma (code-to-design)
- The user wants to update, sync, or edit an existing Figma file
- The user shares a figma.com URL
- The user wants to build or extend a design system, design tokens, or component library
- The user wants to create a diagram in FigJam

SKILLS (Prefer the skills shipped with the Figma plugin on the agent being used. If no Figma plugin is installed, use the skills served by the Figma MCP resource):
- /figma-use — MANDATORY before calling use_figma; fallback: skill://figma/figma-use/SKILL.md
- /figma-generate-design — for translating an app page or layout into Figma; fallback: skill://figma/figma-generate-design/SKILL.md

## claude.ai Microsoft Learn
# Microsoft Learn MCP Server

This server gives structured access to official Microsoft and Azure documentation via three tools:

## Tools

### microsoft_docs_search
Search official documentation and return up to 10 concise, high-quality content chunks (max 500 tokens each), including title, URL, and excerpt.

- Use first to get a quick, reliable overview
- Ideal for grounding answers in Microsoft knowledge

### microsoft_code_sample_search
Search for code snippets and examples in official Microsoft Learn documentation and return up to 20 relevant, high-quality code samples.

- Use when you need to provide sample Microsoft/Azure related code in your answers.  
- Ideal for generating code snippets or practical implementation examples.  
- Optional parameter `language` can filter results. 

### microsoft_docs_fetch
Fetch and convert full Microsoft documentation pages to markdown.

- Use after search when you need full content from a specific URL
- Required for detailed tutorials, troubleshooting, prerequisites, code samples, or when search results are incomplete or outdated

## Workflow

1. Use `microsoft_docs_search` to find relevant documents.
2. If you need code examples or practical snippets, use `microsoft_code_sample_search`.
3. If deeper or complete information is needed, use `microsoft_docs_fetch`.

**Search gives breadth. Code Sample Search gives practical examples. Fetch gives depth.**

All content comes from Microsoft Learn or official sources, returned in clean markdown format.

## claude.ai tldraw
Use `search` to query the tldraw Editor API spec (e.g. search for methods by category or name). Use `exec` to run JavaScript on the canvas — your code receives `editor` (the tldraw Editor instance) and helpers like toRichText, createShapeId, createArrowBetweenShapes. The current canvas state is kept in model context as raw TLShape, asset, and binding data.

## plugin:small-business:gmail
This is an MCP server provided by Gmail API. The server provides tools for developers to build LLM applications on top of Gmail.

## plugin:small-business:shopify
This server helps users set up and manage their Shopify stores.

## Store Creation
Users who don't have a store yet can use get-new-store-previews to create one from a short description.
After calling get-new-store-previews, encourage the user to browse the previews and pick the theme they like best.
Each preview has a signup link — signing up through it creates a real Shopify store with that theme and matching products pre-installed.
Encourage continued brainstorming: users can try different descriptions, tweak ideas, or explore new directions without commitment.

## Store Management
Once a store exists, this server provides tools for managing it:
- Products: search, create, update, bulk-update status, and organize into collections.
- Collections: search, create, update, and manage product groupings.
- Orders: list recent orders and get detailed order information.
- Customers: list and search customers.
- Inventory: check inventory levels and set quantities at specific locations.
- Analytics: run ShopifyQL queries for sales, order, and product performance data.
- Discounts: create percentage-based discount codes.

## GraphQL — General-Purpose Access
The Shopify Admin API exposes hundreds of resources. The built-in tools above are optimized shortcuts for common operations (with structured output and widgets), but they only cover a subset of the API.
When the user asks about a resource that has no dedicated built-in tool — such as gift cards, metafields, metaobjects, pages, blogs, markets, translations, publications, and many others — fulfill the request with the GraphQL Workflow below. NEVER tell the user that data is unavailable just because there is no built-in tool for it.

Decision logic:
1. If a built-in tool matches the request, prefer it (better UX).
2. If no built-in tool matches, run the GraphQL Workflow below. Do NOT open with graphql_query or graphql_mutation — the workflow starts at graphql_schema.

Based on the web search results, here's what I found about the BGH decision on Baukostenzuschuss for battery storage:

## BGH Decision on Battery Storage Construction Cost Allowances

The BGH decided on July 15, 2025 (case number EnVR 1/24) that grid operators are permitted to charge construction cost allowances (Baukostenzuschüsse) for the grid connection of battery storage systems according to the performance price model.

### Key Details:

According to the BGH's assessment, charging a construction cost allowance based on the performance price model for grid-connected battery storage systems is not discriminatory under § 17 paragraph 1 of the Energy Industry Act (EnWG) and is therefore generally permitted.

A construction cost allowance (BKZ) is a one-time cost contribution that occurs when a grid connection requires additional expansion or reinforcement of the electricity network, not for ongoing network usage but for the technical enablement of the connection itself.

### Background:

The case involved an operator of battery storage systems and a grid operator, with the Higher Regional Court (OLG) Düsseldorf initially ruling in favor of the company, though the BGH did not follow this assessment. The detailed decision reasons were published a week later, on July 22, 2025.

## Network Charge Exemption Overview

New electrical energy storage facilities that are put into operation by August 4, 2029 are exempted from network access charges for a period of 20 years from commissioning for the procurement of electrical energy to be stored.

## Eligibility Window

The privilege applies to all facilities for storing electrical energy newly constructed after December 31, 2008, that are put into operation between August 4, 2011 within an 18-year period, meaning all battery storage facilities put into operation between August 4, 2011 and August 4, 2029.

## What Qualifies as Commissioning

A power storage facility is considered to be in operation when it draws electricity for the first time for test operation.

## Regulatory Authority's Deviation Powers

The deviation authority in § 118 Abs. 6 S. 12 EnWG allows both substantive changes and, in particular, a new regulation regarding "the temporal scope" of network charge exemptions. The Federal Network Agency was given authority through § 118 Abs. 6 Sentence 12 EnWG to deviate from the statutory network charge exemption through regulation, including with respect to its temporal scope.

This means the August 4, 2029 deadline may potentially be subject to modification by regulatory decision.

Based on the web search results, here's comprehensive information about battery storage privilege in outdoor areas under § 35 BauGB 2025:

## Overview of the Legal Changes

To accelerate the approval of large-scale battery storage systems in outdoor areas, a privilege was decided through § 35 Abs. 1 Nr. 11 in the Building Code (BauGB) in November 2025. However, the situation is more complex due to recent legislative changes.

## Two-Phase Legislation

The EnWG amendment of November 13, 2025 initially brought a flat rate privilege for systems of 1 MWh or more, which was later replaced by the Geothermal Acceleration Act of December 4, 2025 with a two-track regulation.

## Current Privilege Framework (as of January 1, 2026)

The Bundestag restricted the originally far-reaching privilege to two privilege provisions: § 35 Abs. 1 Nr. 11 BauGB for co-location battery storage in spatial-functional connection with an existing renewable energy facility, and § 35 Abs. 1 Nr. 12 BauGB for other battery storage systems not covered by number 11.

## Key Conditions and Limitations

The total area used by all battery storage systems approved under this provision in the same municipality must not exceed 0.5 percent of the municipality's area and may be at most 50,000 m².

## Practical Impact

The privilege shortens approval from typically 18 to 36 months (development plan procedure) to 6 to 9 months (building permit), but only for projects meeting narrow cumulative thresholds.

Despite these adjustments, many actors still face uncertainty about practical implementation, with further clarifications from the federal government needed.

# § 118 Abs. 6 EnWG - Netzentgeltbefreiung für Speicher

**Satz 1-3:**
"Nach dem 31. Dezember 2008 neu errichtete Anlagen zur Speicherung elektrischer Energie, die ab 4. August 2011, innerhalb von 18 Jahren in Betrieb genommen werden, sind für einen Zeitraum von 20 Jahren ab Inbetriebnahme hinsichtlich des Bezugs der zu speichernden elektrischen Energie von den Entgelten für den Netzzugang freigestellt."

Die Regelung betrifft modernisierte Pumpspeicherkraftwerke mit nachgewiesen um mindestens 7,5 Prozent erhöhter Leistung oder um mindestens 5 Prozent erhöhter Speicherkapazität – diese erhalten eine Befreiungsdauer von zehn Jahren ab Inbetriebnahme.

**Satz 12:**
"Auf Grundlage von § 21 Absatz 3 Satz 3 Nummer 3 kann die Regulierungsbehörde von den Sätzen 1 bis 11 abweichende Regelungen treffen, insbesondere zum zeitlichen Anwendungsbereich, zu den zu erfüllenden Voraussetzungen und zum Ausgleich entgangener Erlöse."

# Entscheidung des Bundesgerichtshofs zu Baukostenzuschüssen für Batteriespeicher

**Datum:** 15. Juli 2025

**Aktenzeichen:** EnVR 1/24

**Kernaussage:** Der Bundesgerichtshof bestätigte, dass Netzbetreiber berechtigt sind, Baukostenzuschüsse nach dem Leistungspreismodell auch für netzgekoppelte Batteriespeicher zu erheben. Die Beschwerde des Antragstellers gegen die Bundesnetzagentur wurde zurückgewiesen.

**Leistungspreismodell:** Das Modell berechnet Baukostenzuschüsse basierend auf der maximalen Leistungskapazität. Die Höhe richtet sich nach dem örtlichen Leistungspreis und soll Anschlussnehmende anreizen, realistische Leistungsbedarfe anzumelden, um unnötige Netzausbaukosten zu vermeiden.

**Zu Bundesnetzagentur (BNetzA):** Das Gericht bescheinigte der BNetzA Entscheidungsspielraum bei der Regulierung. Die BNetzA durfte davon ausgehen, dass das Leistungspreismodell trotz Unterschieden zwischen Batteriespeichern und anderen Verbrauchern gerechtfertigt ist.

# § 35 Abs. 1 BauGB - Solar- und Speicheranlagen

## Nummern 8, 9, 11, 12 (Wortlaut)

**Nr. 8:** "der Nutzung solarer Strahlungsenergie dient" auf Dächern/Außenwänden oder "längs von Autobahnen oder Schienenwegen des übergeordneten Netzes" in max. 200 m Entfernung.

**Nr. 9:** "der Nutzung solarer Strahlungsenergie durch besondere Solaranlagen" mit räumlich-funktionalem Zusammenhang zu Betrieben, max. 25.000 qm Grundfläche, eine Anlage je Hofstelle.

**Nr. 11:** "der Speicherung von elektrischer Energie in einer Batteriespeicheranlage" mit räumlich-funktionalem Zusammenhang zu bestehenden Erneuerbare-Energien-Anlagen.

**Nr. 12:** Batteriespeicher ohne Erneuerbaren-Bezug mit drei Bedingungen:

1. **Lage:** max. 200 m zur Grundstücksgrenze einer Umspannanlage (Höchst-/Hochspannung oder Hochspannung/Mittelspannung) oder Kraftwerk (≥50 MW)
2. **Kapazität:** mind. 4 Megawatt Nennleistung
3. **Fläche:** Gesamtfläche aller Anlagen in der Gemeinde max. 0,5 % der Gemeindefläche, höchstens 50.000 qm

## Key Findings on Battery Storage Revenues 2025

FCR revenues in the 2-hour system declined by over 90 percent and play barely any role in the optimized schedule, while aFRR Capacity revenues increased by 40 percent in the 2-hour system and established themselves as a new revenue anchor.

**Annual Revenue Potential (€/MW/year):**
The revenue potential for 2025 was approximately €260,000 per MW per year for a 2-hour system according to the ISEA Index, though well-marketed large storage systems typically realize about 80% of this.

**Market Shifts:**
In 2025, there were three core drivers of battery storage revenues with approximately 25% share each: continuous intraday trading, positive aFRR market, and negative aFRR market. The aFRR Energy segment saw particularly significant declines, with the 2-hour system losing 65.3 percent of its revenues.

**Future Outlook:**
No trend reversal in declining FCR prices is expected, since supply growth in Germany has been significantly stronger than demand growth.

## Key Findings:

**Positionspapier and Regulatory Framework:**
The 8th Decision Chamber of the Bundesnetzagentur released a position paper in November 2024 to specifically regulate the Baukostenzuschuss (BKZ) for network connections. The BKZ for network levels above low voltage is oriented towards the "Position Paper on the Levy of Construction Cost Contributions" from the Decision Chamber 8 of the Bundesnetzagentur from 2024.

**Storage and Grid-Serving Behavior:**
Regulatory options are being considered that minimally impair storage operation in their respective dispatch modes, while enabling storage operators as network users to participate in financing network costs and simultaneously creating incentives for grid-serving usage behavior.

**Differentiated BKZ Approach:**
Differentiation can occur when the settlement of a consumer - such as a factory, electrolyzer, or storage facility - from a network perspective causes no additional costs or fewer costs at a particular location. Operators of electrolyzers or large battery storage systems should settle primarily in regions with sufficient network capacity through discounts on connection costs.

**2026 Implementation:**
As of January 1, 2026, the BKZ for network levels above low voltage follows the 2024 position paper from the Bundesnetzagentur's Decision Chamber 8.

# Großbatteriespeicher in Deutschland - Stichpunkte

## Installierte Leistung & Prognosen
- **Aktuell (15.10.2025)**: ~2,4 GW Bruttoleistung, ~3,2 GWh nutzbare Speicherkapazität
- **In Planung**: ~5,0 GW Bruttoleistung, ~10,4 GWh Speicherkapazität
- **Prognose 2037**: 41,1–94,1 GW (Szenariorahmen 2025-2037/2045)
- **Prognose 2045**: 41,1–94,1 GW

## Netzanschlussanfragen
- Ende 2024: "bereits rund 650 Anschlussanfragen für Großbatteriespeicher mit einer Gesamtleistung von 226 GW" bei Übertragungsnetzbetreibern

## Netzanschluss - Regulatorische Besonderheiten
- **KraftNAV nicht anwendbar** (seit Verordnung 23.12.2025)
- Speicher benötigen Kapazität für Ein- und Ausspeisung
- **Flexible Connection Agreements (FCA)** möglich – auch dauerhaft
- **Realisierungskautionen**: ~1.500 Euro/MW gelten als angemessen

## Baukostenzuschuss (BKZ)
- Ja, auch für netzgekoppelte Batteriespeicher oberhalb Niederspannung
- **Keine Ermäßigung** wegen Speicherfunktion – volle Höhe fällig
- BKZ kann durch FCA reduziert werden (sachlich begründet)

## Betrieb – Entflechtungsregeln
- Netzbetreiber dürfen Speicher grundsätzlich **nicht besitzen**
- Ausnahmen nur mit BNetzA-Genehmigung nach erfolglosem Markttest
- **Batteriespeicher können keine vollständig integrierten Netzkomponenten sein**

# BNetzA's AgNes Plans for Storage Network Charges

## Current Status (May 2026 Interim Report)

The Federal Network Agency has shifted toward **stronger trust protection** for storage operators. According to their position:

- Full 20-year exemption is retained for those making investment decisions **before the final AgNes ruling takes effect** and placing storage online **by August 3, 2029**
- This applies to both existing and new projects

## Charges After 2029

New storage facilities that miss the trust protection window will face:
- **Capacity charge:** approximately €4–7 per kilowatt annually (fixed fee, not usage-based)
- **Work charges:** none
- **Exemption:** residential storage in low-voltage grids remains excluded

## Timeline

The regulator aims for a **final, binding determination by end of 2026**, with formal public consultation launching summer 2026. Companies seeking full exemption should document investment decisions **this year** to qualify for protection.

## Key Uncertainty

While the interim report provides clearer guidance than earlier 2025–early 2026 positions (which questioned the exemption entirely), the final ruling remains pending and represents the legally binding standard.

## Key Points for Battery Storage Reimbursement

Storage operators with end consumption can request reimbursement of network usage fees from the network operator (VNB) as of January 1, 2026.

**Important Distinction Between Storage Types:**

- Storage without end consumption has been exempt from network usage fees since January 1, 2025.
- For storage with end consumption, the fee is reimbursed proportionally for the electricity quantity fed back into the network.

**Requirements for Reimbursement:**

The reimbursement applies only to the electricity quantity that is drawn from the network, stored, and later fed back into the network. This requires a suitable metering system that clearly documents how much electricity was loaded from and fed back into the network.

**Stationary vs. Mobile Storage:**

For stationary storage, only the electricity that was previously loaded from the network is reimbursed, while for mobile storage (such as electric vehicles with bidirectional charging capability), the entire electricity is reimbursed.

The regulations are based on the revised Stromversorgungsverordnung (StromVV), specifically Articles 18c-18i, which came into force on February 19, 2025.

content.content:
# Steuerbefreiung für Erneuerbare Energien nach § 9 StromStG

**§ 9 Abs. 1 Nr. 1** (Große Anlagen):
Strom aus Windkraft, Sonnenenergie, Erdwärme oder Wasserkraft in Anlagen über 2 Megawatt ist befreit, wenn er "vom Betreiber der Anlage am Ort der Erzeugung zum Selbstverbrauch entnommen wird" – jedoch nur bei lokaler Nutzung ohne Netzeinspeisung.

**§ 9 Abs. 1 Nr. 3** (Kleine Anlagen):
Strom aus erneuerbaren Quellen oder KWK-Anlagen bis 2 Megawatt unterliegt einer Steuerbefreiung unter zwei Bedingungen:

- Der Betreiber nutzt den Strom selbst „im räumlichen Zusammenhang zu der Anlage", oder
- Der Betreiber liefert den Strom an Letztverbraucher in räumlicher Nähe zur Anlage

## Solar-PPA Preise Deutschland 2026

Der deutsche Markt für Solar-PPAs hat 2026 institutionelle Reife erreicht. Corporate-PPAs machen 2026 rund 78 % des PPA-Marktes aus.

### Preisangaben nach Struktur:

Pay-as-Produced 10-Jahre kostet 5,3 bis 7,2 ct/kWh, während Sleeved-PPAs 5,9 bis 7,4 ct/kWh betragen.

### Marktstruktur und Volumen:

Pay-as-Produced bleibt dominante Struktur (rund 64 % der Neuverträge), Baseload-PPAs nur mit ergänzender Speicher- oder Hybrid-Struktur, Floor-Strukturen mit Mindestpreis 3,8–4,5 ct/kWh werden Standard.

Es wird erwartet, dass 6,5–8,0 GWp neue Solar-PPAs in 2026 abgeschlossen werden.

content.content:
# § 15 Abs. 3 und 4 GmbHG - Notarielle Form bei Abtretung

**Absatz 3:**
"Zur Abtretung von Geschäftsanteilen durch Gesellschafter bedarf es eines in notarieller Form geschlossenen Vertrags."

This provision requires that any transfer of business shares must be documented through a notarized contract.

**Absatz 4:**
"Der notariellen Form bedarf auch eine Vereinbarung, durch welche die Verpflichtung eines Gesellschafters zur Abtretung eines Geschäftsanteils begründet wird."

This clause extends the notarization requirement to agreements establishing an obligation to transfer shares. However, the provision includes an important exception: informal agreements become valid once the actual transfer contract (meeting formal requirements) is executed.

**Practical effect:** Both the transfer itself and any prior binding commitment to transfer shares require notarial certification under German GmbH law.

# German Real Estate Transfer Tax (GrEStG) - Key Thresholds

According to § 1 of the Grunderwerbsteuergesetz, the legislation establishes important thresholds for taxing ownership changes in companies holding domestic properties:

**90% Threshold:**
When "mindestens 90 vom Hundert der Anteile" (at least 90% of shares) transfer to new shareholders in either a partnership or corporation owning German real estate, this triggers transfer tax liability.

**10-Year Window:**
This 90% threshold is measured "innerhalb von zehn Jahren" (within a ten-year period), allowing tax authorities to aggregate ownership changes across a decade to determine if the trigger has been met.

**Scope:**
The rules apply to both direct and indirect ownership transitions, with special provisions for multi-layered corporate structures. Publicly traded shares are excluded from this calculation when traded on regulated markets.

The provision effectively prevents tax avoidance through fragmented share transfers and ensures taxation when effective control of property-holding entities shifts substantially.

content.content:
# § 1090 BGB – Beschränkte persönliche Dienstbarkeit

## Wortlaut
Nach § 1090 Abs. 1 BGB kann ein Grundstück belastet werden, sodass der Berechtigte das Grundstück "in einzelnen Beziehungen zu benutzen" oder eine "sonstige Befugnis" hat, die einer Grunddienstbarkeit entspricht.

## Übertragbarkeit
Die bereitgestellte Quelle behandelt § 1092 Abs. 3 BGB nicht. Der Text erwähnt nur, dass die §§ 1020-1024, 1026-1029 und 1061 BGB entsprechend anwendbar sind (Abs. 2), gibt aber keine Auskunft zur Übertragbarkeit auf juristische Personen.

Für Details zur Transferierbarkeit dieser Dienstbarkeit auf juristische Personen wären weitere Rechtsquellen erforderlich.

# Planungsrechtliche Voraussetzungen für Freiflächenanlagen nach § 37 EEG 2023

## Bebauungsplan-Anforderungen

Gebote erfordern einen beschlossenen Bebauungsplan, der entweder:
- vor dem 1. September 2003 aufgestellt wurde (ohne nachträgliche Änderung zum Solaranlagenbau), oder
- vor dem 1. Januar 2010 ein Gewerbe- oder Industriegebiet ausgewiesen hatte

## Zulässige Flächenkategorien

Die Anlagen dürfen nur auf folgenden Flächen errichtet werden:

1. **Bereits versiegelte Flächen** zum Zeitpunkt des Bebauungsplanbeschlusses
2. **Konversionsflächen** aus wirtschaftlicher, verkehrlicher oder militärischer Nutzung
3. **Autobahn-/Schienennähe**: bis 500 Meter Entfernung
4. **Gewerbe-/Industriegebiete** (vor 2010 ausgewiesen)
5. **Ackerflächen oder Grünland** in benachteiligten Gebieten (mit Naturschutzausschlüssen)
6. **Bundesliegenschaften**, die zur Solarentwicklung veröffentlicht wurden

Moorböden sind grundsätzlich ausgeschlossen, außer bei geplanter Wiedervernässung.

content.content:
# § 1092 BGB: Übertragbarkeit beschränkter persönlicher Dienstbarkeiten

**Abs. 1 - Grundregel:**
"Eine beschränkte persönliche Dienstbarkeit ist nicht übertragbar." Die Ausübung kann jedoch an andere überlassen werden, sofern dies zulässig ist.

**Abs. 3 - Ausnahme für juristische Personen:**
Für juristische Personen und rechtsfähige Personengesellschaften gibt es eine wichtige Ausnahme: Eine beschränkte persönliche Dienstbarkeit wird übertragbar, wenn sie die Nutzung eines Grundstücks für folgende Zwecke berechtigt:

1. Erneuerbare Energieanlagen (Wasserkraft, Wind, Solar, Geothermie, Biomasse)
2. Wasserstoff-Anlagen
3. Versorgungsleitungen (Strom, Gas, Wasser, Abwasser, Öl, Rohstoffe)
4. Telekommunikationsanlagen
5. Produkttransportanlagen zwischen Betriebsstätten
6. Straßenbahn- oder Eisenbahnanlagen

Die Übertragbarkeit umfasst nicht das Recht zur Aufteilung der Dienstbarkeit nach ihren Befugnissen.

I've completed a web search for your query about the Umweltbundesamt (German Federal Environment Agency), the HKNR (Herkunftsnachweisregister - Register of Guarantees of Origin), and related topics in German renewable energy regulation.

Here's a summary of the key findings:

## HKNR - Herkunftsnachweisregister (Register of Guarantees of Origin)

The Umweltbundesamt (UBA) operates the Herkunftsnachweisregister (HKNR) for green electricity sold in Germany. The Register of Guarantees of Origin (HKNR) went into operation on 1 January 2013.

## What are Herkunftsnachweise (Guarantees of Origin)?

The Herkunftsnachweis is an electronic document that functions like a birth certificate. It certifies how and where electricity from renewable energies was produced. Simultaneously, this document ensures that this quality can only be sold once.

## Doppelvermarktungsverbot (Double Marketing Prohibition)

Under German law, plant operators can choose whether to claim EEG funding for the electricity they generate (in which case it is automatically purchased) or to receive Herkunftsnachweise instead in order to achieve profits through their marketing (double marketing prohibition). 

To prevent federally subsidized electricity in Germany from being sold again – in addition to the obligatory assignment – as renewable energy, it receives no guarantees of origin. Guarantees of origin are only issued in Germany for renewable electricity generation that does not receive subsidies.

The HKNR monitors the marketing of this electricity and will reliably exclude double marketing through guarantees of origin.

Based on the search results, here is information about § 76 GmbHG Österreich regarding the Notariatsakt requirement for the transfer of business shares:

## Key Requirements

For the transfer of business shares by legal transaction inter vivos, a notarial deed is required. Agreements about the obligation of a shareholder to transfer a business share in the future require the same form.

## Scope of the Form Requirement

In the articles of association, the transfer of business shares can be made dependent on further conditions, particularly on the approval of the company.

The right to transfer also includes the right to pledge contractually, though the latter does not require a notarial deed.

## Purposes of the Notarial Deed Requirement

According to Austrian case law, the form requirement serves multiple functions:

1. Immobilization: Business shares should not become the subject of commercial traffic.
2. Proof security: Clarity regarding economic allocation and ensuring the identity of the respective shareholder.
3. Protection against hasty action: The acquirer should be made aware of the risks associated with acquiring a stake in a capital company.

The official Austrian RIS (Rechtsinformationssystem) database contains the complete and current text of § 76 GmbHG if you need the full statutory language.

content.content:
# Netznutzungsentgelt für Speicher in der Schweiz

## Speicher ohne Endverbrauch (seit 2025)
Reine Speicher sind grundsätzlich vom Netznutzungsentgelt befreit. Dies gilt für alle Tarifkomponenten einschließlich Grund- und Leistungstarif sowie Systemdienstleistungen.

## Speicher mit Endverbrauch (ab 2026)
Betreiber erhalten eine teilweise Rückerstattung: "das Netznutzungsentgelt für die Elektrizitätsmenge zurückerstattet wird, die nach dem Bezug aus dem Netz und nach der Speicherung zurückgespeist wird."

Die Rückerstattung gilt nur für die **Arbeitskomponente** (Rp./kWh), nicht für Grund- oder Leistungstarife. Sie basiert auf dem Durchschnittstarif des Tarifjahrs am jeweiligen Netzanschlusspunkt.

## Messkosten
Speicher mit Endverbrauch benötigen ein intelligentes Messsystem, wenn am gleichen Messpunkt auch eine Erzeugungsanlage installiert ist. Die Betreiber tragen diese Messkosten selbst.

## Rechtsgrundlage
Artikel 14a des Stromversorgungsgesetzes (StromVG) und die entsprechende Verordnung (StromVV).

**Der Preis folgt dem Risiko:** Für eine reine Flächensicherung werden oft nur 5–20 €/kWp gezahlt, für baureife Projekte (RTB) 60–130 €/kWp – Orientierungswerte DACH, Stand 2026.
Üblich ist der **Share Deal**: Der Käufer übernimmt die Projektgesellschaft (SPV) mit allen Pacht-, Netz- und Planungsrechten. Ein Asset Deal ist möglich, aber aufwendiger.
Käufer früher Phasen sichern sich über **Meilensteinzahlungen und Earn-outs** ab: Gezahlt wird erst, wenn Satzungsbeschluss, Netzzusage oder Baugenehmigung tatsächlich vorliegen.
Die Due Diligence entscheidet über den Preis. Die häufigsten Deal-Breaker sind **lückenhafte Flächensicherung, eine unsichere Netzanschlusszusage und ein angreifbarer Bebauungsplan**.
Über die [Projektbörse](/projektboerse) ist die Suche für Investoren kostenfrei; Verkäufer zahlen 1,5–3 % des Kaufpreises, nur bei erfolgreichem Abschluss.
grossspeicher-erloese words 1896 min 9 title 63 seo 44 desc 159 faq 6 quellen 8 intLinks 11 tabellen 3
Ein Großspeicher verdient an **Preisunterschieden (Arbitrage) und an Regelenergie**. Realistisch sind nach unserer Annahme 90.000–180.000 € je MW und Jahr für einen 2-Stunden-Speicher.
Die Erlöse sinken: Der Erlösindex der RWTH Aachen fiel für 2-h-Systeme von 309.000 € (2024) auf 259.000 € je MW (2025) – vor allem, weil der Primärregelmarkt (FCR) gesättigt ist.
Systempreise fallen ebenfalls: rund 200–340 €/kWh schlüsselfertig. Im Beispiel 10 MW/20 MWh ergibt das eine Projektrendite von etwa **6,4 % bis 23,9 %** vor Steuern und Finanzierung.
Der Engpass ist der **Netzanschluss**: 2025 wurden 573,5 GW Speicherleistung angefragt, aber nur 54,2 GW zugesagt. Baukostenzuschüsse sind laut BGH (Juli 2025) zulässig.
Speicher, die bis **4. August 2029** in Betrieb gehen, bleiben nach § 118 Abs. 6 EnWG 20 Jahre von Netzentgelten für den Strombezug befreit – nach dem aktuellen AgNes-Stand der Bundesnetzagentur mit Vertrauensschutz.
ppa-fuer-unternehmen words 1834 min 9 title 60 seo 52 desc 158 faq 6 quellen 6 intLinks 10 tabellen 4
Ein **PPA (Power Purchase Agreement)** ist ein langfristiger Liefervertrag direkt mit einem Erzeuger – meist über 3 bis 15 Jahre, zu einem festen oder begrenzten Preis.
Solar-PPAs mit 10 Jahren Laufzeit lagen 2025 laut dena-Marktanalyse indikativ bei **35–45 €/MWh** (3,5–4,5 ct/kWh) auf Erzeugerebene. Für Abnehmer kommen Kosten für Strukturierung und Ausgleich hinzu.
Der Preis ist nicht alles: Ein Solar-PPA liefert **mittags viel und nachts nichts**. Das Profil-, Volumen- und Kreditrisiko entscheidet, ob sich der Vertrag rechnet.
Produzierendes Gewerbe zahlt seit 1. Januar 2026 dauerhaft nur noch **0,05 ct/kWh Stromsteuer** statt 2,05 ct (über den Entlastungsantrag).
Off-site-PPAs lohnen sich in der Regel erst bei größeren Mengen. Für kleinere Betriebe kann ein **gebündelter Einkauf** die Alternative sein.
